newsitem.title: UK: TIMELINES - Today in History - Aug 20.
newsitem.headline: TIMELINES - Today in History - Aug 20.

text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
English novelist EMILY BRONTE was born in 1818. Her only book was "Wuthering Heights" which wasn't a success until after her death. Her sister CHARLOTTE was the family best-seller.
The Australian etcher and painter SYDNEY LONG was born in 1871.
Australian politician JAMES "Digger" DUNN was born in 1887. He earned a reputation as a vitriolic speaker with comments such as "a political turkey-cock" and "a mind as dirty and filthy as a sewer."
U.S. horror story writer H.P. LOVECRAFT was born in 1890.
The Australian featherweight and lightweight boxing champion SIDNEY GODFREY was born in 1897. He was known as the "K.O. King".
Australian atomic scientist and Governor of South Australia Sir MARK OLIPHANT was born in 1901.
American jazz trombone player and singer JACK TEAGARDEN was born in 1905.
British tennis player BUNNY AUSTIN, who won the Davis Cup four times, was born in 1906.

American country and western singer JIM (JAMES TRAVIS) REEVES was born in 1924. But for an ankle injury, he may have become a great baseball player. He died when his private plane crashed on the 31st of July, 1964.

American novelist JACQUELINE SUSANN was born in 1926. Her "Valley of the Dolls" style was parodied in a hugely successful literary hoax, when 24 journalists wrote "Naked Came the Stranger". They wrote the formula book, including one sex scene per 15 pages and 12 four-letter words per chapter.

American singer and pianist ISAAC HAYES, who started as a session musician with OTIS REDDING, was born in 1942. He wrote a number of hits including "Soul Man" and "Hold On, I'm Coming" with DAVID PORTER, and his biggest hit was "The Theme From Shaft" (1971).

British singer/songwriter ROBERT PLANT, who made his recording debut in 1966 with the group 'Listen', was born in 1948. He joined the 'New Yardbirds' with JIMMY PAGE and JOHN BONHAM, before PAGE heard a quote by KEITH MOON (drummer with 'The Who') that he liked ... " going down like a lead Zeppelin",
and renamed the band 'Led Zeppelin'. Their best known hit was "Stairway To Heaven", and following the death of BONHAM (September 25th, 1980), PLANT went solo.
British singer with the band 'Thin Lizzy', PHIL LYNOTT, was born in 1951. He died on the 4th of January, 1986, after being in a coma for a week.
** EVENTS **
1741 : Alaska was discovered by Danish explorer VITUS
BERING.
1857 : The "DUNBAR" struck rocks off Sydney's South Head,

and of the 63 passengers and 59 crew, there was only one survivor. A man named JOHNSON was hauled to safety after clinging to a rock for 36 hours. Bodies were washed up on Sydney beaches for days. More than 20,000 people attended the mass burial of those who could not be identified.
1860 : The Great Northern Exploration led by BURKE and

WILLS set out to cross Australia from south to north. From a camp at Cooper's Creek BURKE and WILLS took six camels, a horse and two fellow explorers GRAY and KING, to walk more than 2,400 kilometres to the Gulf of Carpentaria. They made it to the tidal waters of the Gulf but during the slow struggle back to the base camp, GRAY died. When they reached the camp it was deserted. BURKE and WILLS later died. KING was helped to survive by Aborigines and was found by a rescue party.
1912 : The British founder of the Salvation Army, WILLIAM
BOOTH, died.
1913 : The first parachute jump was performed by ADOLPHE
PEGOND, who baled out of an aircraft at 213 metres, and parachuted safely to the ground.
1913 : Stainless steel was cast for the first time at
Sheffield.
1924 : British runner ERIC LIDDEL refused to compete in
the 100 metres at the Paris Olympics on religious grounds because the event was held on a Sunday.
1940 : Radar was used for the first time by the British
during World War Two.
1940 : LEON TROTSKY, Russian revolutionary, was fatally
wounded by a Spanish communist with an ice axe in Mexico City, dying the next day. The Soviet government denied responsibility.
1940 - As the Battle of Britain raged, Prime Minister WINSTON CHURCHILL told parliament "Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few".
1941 : Australian country singer SMOKEY DAWSON attended
his first recording session at Sydney's Columbia studios where he sang "I'm a Happy-Go-Lucky Cowhand".
1944 - U.S. and British forces destroyed the German Seventh Army at Falaise-Argentan Gap, west of Paris, capturing 50,000 Germans.
1961 : East Germany began to erect a five-foot high wall
along the border with the west to replace the barbed wire put up on August 13.
1968 : Soviet and Warsaw Pact troops crossed the border
into Czechoslovakia just before midnight at the start of the invasion to crush the "Prague Spring" reforms.
1969 : MICK JAGGER was accidentally shot while filming
"Ned Kelly" in Australia.
1970 : American Lieutenant JAMES CALLEY had his sentence
for the My Lai massacre in Vietnam reduced by 20 years, after public claims that he was being made a scapegoat.
1980 : The first successful ascent of Mount Everest by a
solo climber was achieved by Italian REINHOLD MESSNER.
1988 : The Iran-Iraqi ceasfire took effect.
1989 : A birthday party on a pleasure boat on London's
Thames River ended in disaster when the vessel was run into by a sand dredger. The party boat, the "Marchioness", sank within minutes, trapping those below deck, killing 51 people.
1991 - The parliament in the Baltic republic of Estonia declared immediate full independence from the Soviet Union.
1995 : At least 350 people were killed in India's worst
train disaster when two Delhi-bound trains collided at Firozobad, 200 km (125 miles) from the Indian capital.
